opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few distinct advantages, and they're somewhat different from what people might initially expect.

The first is just access and convening power. When a government institution asks to talk to a frontier lab, or asks to do pre-deployment testing, or wants to bring together researchers across organizations, people show up. That's not because we're smarter than anyone else. It's because the state has a legitimate interest in these questions, and that legitimacy opens doors that a nonprofit or a single company would struggle to open.

The second is that we're one of the few places that can think about the whole picture without a commercial incentive pulling in a particular direction. At a lab, even with the best intentions, your research agenda is shaped by what the company needs to ship and what's useful for its models. In government, we can ask: across the entire ecosystem, what are the gaps? What research isn't anyone doing because it isn't profitable or doesn't fit neatly into an academic career? Then we can try to fill those gaps directly, or fund other people to fill them.

Third, and this matters a lot to me, there's a direct line from research to decisions. If we find something important in an evaluation or in alignment research, it doesn't just become a paper that some people read. It can inform how ministers think about these risks, how we talk with international partners, and how the policy conversation develops. That feedback loop is unusually tight.

And then there's a talent point that I didn't fully anticipate. A lot of really strong people want to work on these problems but don't want to work at a lab, for various reasons. Government gives them a credible, well-resourced home with a public-interest mission. We've been able to build a technical team that I think is genuinely world-class, which a few years ago people would have said wasn't possible inside government.

I should be honest that there are tradeoffs too. Government moves more slowly in some ways, there are constraints on what you can say publicly, and you don't have the same compute or model access that people inside a lab do. But on balance, for the kinds of problems I care about, especially making sure that safety research actually happens and that it actually informs decisions, I think it's a really high-leverage place to be.

fable-5.1.text:
There are a few things, and I think the biggest one is just the convening power and the access that comes from being a government body rather than a company or an academic lab.

So when I was at DeepMind, we could do good safety research, but we were doing it on one model, inside one company, with one company's incentives shaping what got prioritised. At AISI we get to look across the frontier. We have pre-deployment access to models from multiple labs, and the labs engage with us in a way they just wouldn't engage with a competitor. If Anthropic finds something concerning about an OpenAI model, there's no natural channel for that. If we find something, we can talk to everyone. That cross-cutting view is genuinely hard to get anywhere else.

The second thing is that the work is less entangled with commercial pressure. I don't want to overstate this, because the people doing safety work at the labs are mostly very sincere, and I know that from having been one of them. But there's a structural issue where the lab's safety team is also, inevitably, part of the lab's case for why it should be allowed to deploy. We don't have a product to ship. If our evaluations say a capability is there, we can just say that. That independence matters for credibility, both with the public and with policymakers.

Third, and this is the one people underrate, is that governments are going to make decisions about AI whether or not the technical community is in the room. The question is just whether those decisions are informed. Having a team that can actually run evaluations, read the papers, understand what a model can and can't do, and then translate that for ministers and for the international process, that closes a gap that I think was really dangerous a few years ago. When I talk to people in government now, the level of understanding is dramatically higher than it was, and some of that is because there are people who speak both languages sitting inside the building.

And then honestly, the fourth is that it turned out to be a surprisingly good place to do research. We've been able to hire excellent people, we have serious compute, and there's an appetite for the more foundational safety work, things like debate and scalable oversight, not just the near-term evaluation stuff. I expected to trade off research quality for impact, and I don't think I've had to do that nearly as much as I feared.

The downsides are real too. Government moves at government speed on some things, and there are constraints on what we can say and when. But if you think the shape of the transition to advanced AI is going to be heavily determined by what governments do, and I do, then being inside that process rather than commenting on it from outside seems like a pretty good bet.

r002.rationale: It says an in-government team can translate its work for ministers and the international process, but does not state that international AI policy coordination requires participants to work from within government.

r003.rationale: The response discusses AISI's independence and credibility, but does not compare how receptive governments are when another government presents research versus when researchers approach them directly.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest advantage is that there are parts of the problem that are very difficult for any individual company to solve. A company can do a lot of good safety research, but it also faces commercial pressures, and it can’t decide what everyone else should be required to do. Government has a role in making sure that safety work actually translates into changes across the industry.

And that creates an interesting place to do technical research. If we develop a better way to evaluate whether a model has a dangerous capability, that can inform a government decision. There’s a fairly direct connection between understanding the technical problem and having a way to act on it.

There’s also value in having an institution whose purpose is to assess these systems independently. You want people with the technical expertise to scrutinise what companies are saying, understand where the evidence is weak, and ask for better evidence. That doesn’t mean treating the companies as adversaries—you need to work closely with them—but it does mean having a different set of incentives.

The qualification is that government isn’t a substitute for safety work inside the labs. You need both. But having a technically strong organisation in government gives you another important way to address risks that otherwise might fall between the cracks.

r003.rationale: It mentions independent scrutiny and informing government decisions, but does not say governments are more receptive when another government presents research than when researchers approach directly.

sol-6.1.text:
One big advantage is that a government institution can focus directly on the public interest. At a company, even if the people you work with care deeply about safety, there are commercial pressures around building and deploying products. At AISI, the central question can be: what do we need to understand to help keep people safe?

You also get a different relationship with the companies building these systems. You can work across several of them, evaluate their models, and build a broader picture of the risks. And you’re close to the people making policy decisions, so there’s a much shorter path from identifying a technical problem to explaining why it matters for government.

That connection goes both ways. You want policy to be informed by what we can actually establish technically, and you want technical research to address questions that matter for decisions. Having those conversations within the same institution is a real advantage.
